extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century London readers, theatre-goers, and polite society (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and theatrical essays advising readers and performers about taste, stagecraft, character, and private conduct in early-18th-century London society. Emphasises what pleases or offends a polite audience and what constitutes good behaviour and happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive physical acting (use of arms/legs/facial expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: English tragedians should 'make the same use of their Arms and Legs, and inform their Faces with as significant Looks and Passions' as great foreign actors (e.g., Nicolini), thereby giving dignity to thought and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Emulate performers who give 'new Majesty to Kings, Resolution to Heroes, and Softness to Lovers' by using body and face to communicate passion. Anti-pattern: actors with 'forced Thoughts, cold Conceits, and unnatural Expressions' whose performance lacks dignity; actors reduced to the level of an ordinary 'prentice'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of spectacle / avoiding counterfeit performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether a spectacular element (e.g., the stage-lion) is genuinely convincing or merely a sham; audiences judge authenticity of the spectacle as part of its success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: different 'lions' varied in temperament — one was overly testy (overacting), another too meek (underacting). Anti-patterns include performers who break character in private or publicly complain about their part, which undermines the appearance of authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience taste should be governed by common sense rather than mere novelty or coarseness
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint that modern diversions sometimes lack common sense even when they display wit; true good sense is preferable to mere coarse entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Critique of contemporary entertainments suggests patrons and writers should prefer sense and decency over spectacles that pander to gross tastes. Example: public amusements that delight but lack reasonable judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain character-consistency in masquerade and costumed performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who appear in costume (masquerades, masques) should 'be able to say or do things proper for the Dress in which he appears' — preserve the character implied by one's costume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: Rakes dressed as Roman senators, philosophers speechless in costume, a nymph who speaks in 'the pert Stile of the Pit Bawdry'. Recommendation: read source texts (e.g., Arcadia) to inhabit a role convincingly and preserve the masque's decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puppet-show and small entertainments: value surprise and novelty (avoid advance bill of fare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not advertising a bill of fare keeps each scene new and unexpected to the audience, producing greater delight and lively entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr Powell's success by not listing scenes beforehand, creating fresh surprises; contrast with operas whose printed expectations create disappointment when the stage fails to match the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism and scenery must be coherent and consistent ('of a Piece')
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery and stage machinery should be uniform and properly managed to preserve the illusion of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: failing to change side-scenes leads to absurd juxtapositions (e.g., a Prospect of the Ocean in the midst of a delightful Grove; a man appearing in a wig in the middle of the sea). Proper stagecraft requires timely changes and coherent scenic design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animals onstage must be disciplined and suitable for their parts
rubrics_metrics.description: When animals are introduced as actors, they must be trained to perform reliably and fit the role; undisciplined animals can spoil a performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sparrows and chaffinches flying into galleries or putting out candles (failures), versus Powell's pig that is well disciplined and dances a minuet (success). Consider the species and the practicality of their behaviour on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet audience expectations created by advertisements and printed programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Productions that promise certain pageantry or effects in advertized bills should deliver them onstage; failure to do so leads to audience disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a king promised to arrive in a triumphant chariot instead appears on foot; thunder and lightning under-provided compared with expectations. Recommendation: align advertising with achievable stage effects or risk disgruntled patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and vocal suitability for roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocal quality must suit the heroic parts; miscasting (e.g., squeaky/high voices for heroes) undermines characterization — 'by the Squeak of their Voices the Heroes of each are Eunuchs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Ensure voice types and vocal delivery match the dignity and requirements of roles; poor vocal suitability diminishes heroic or serious characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and cultivate elevated manners in masque/assembly to promote refined gallantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Masquerades may form a foundation for 'more elegant and improving Gallantries' if maskers preserve their characters and decorum in assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: encourage maskers to adopt appropriate speech and behaviour for their characters to raise the tone of public amusements rather than degrade them into coarse spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft timing and proportion (special effects should be judicious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects such as thunder, lightning, smoke, or mechanical devices must be executed with due timing and proportion to be effective and not ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: praise for the boy directing painted dragons who 'made them spit Fire and Smoke' in 'just Proportions' and 'in such due Time' — but criticism when an operator reveals his candle or keeps his head improperly. Technical precision enhances belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching or encouraging childish terrors (on ghosts and apparitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adults should not feed children's imaginations with ghost stories that produce persistent fears; a sound imagination and clear judgment are preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: children and even soldiers frightened by shadows or bull-rushes; recommendation to 'arm our selves against them by the Dictates of Reason and Religion' and avoid imbuing the young with absurd terrors.

rubrics_metrics.name: True happiness: private enjoyment, select companionship, and ordered domestic life
rubrics_metrics.description: True happiness arises from enjoying oneself, the friendship of a few companions, privacy, and a regular household economy rather than public display and pomp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of Aurelia: delights in country privacy, mutual esteem with husband, regular hours, and a small household 'like a little Common-Wealth.' Anti-pattern: Fulvia's pursuit of outward display (coaches, lace, ribbons) leading to superficial and fragile felicity.
